title: Alaska Senate Fight Centers on Two Candidates Named Dan Sullivan
summary:
President Donald Trump says he ordered a lawsuit that could block certification of Alaska's Senate election, but only if the Republican incumbent loses. The case, filed by the Justice Department close to Election Day, centers on a ballot with two candidates named Dan Sullivan.

The incumbent is Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, listed as Daniel S. The other candidate is Dan J. Sullivan. Republicans are worried voters could get confused by the similar names. The Alaska Supreme Court has already considered the question and said Dan J. Sullivan could stay on the ballot.

The Justice Department says it filed the lawsuit to protect the integrity of the Senate election. It argued that the federal government could be harmed if certification were tainted by what it called a frivolous candidacy, because that would undermine confidence in the federal government.

President Trump, asked about the case, said he was the one who said to file it. He argued that Democrats had put up a second Dan Sullivan, and he called Daniel J. the fake candidate. The report notes that Daniel J. Sullivan has voted in Alaska races before.

Election expert David Becker, a former Justice Department civil rights attorney, offered a different view. He said the matter is purely one of state law, and that the Justice Department has no authority and no role in it. He also said trying to block certification 11 days before the vote was unprecedented.

The Alaska dispute is part of a final campaign push as Trump works to help Republicans keep control of Congress. Trump is scheduled to campaign in Georgia on Saturday and in Michigan on Sunday, where Republican Mike Rogers faces Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. Former President Barack Obama is also scheduled to campaign in Michigan on Saturday with El-Sayed.
why_it_matters: The case raises questions about who decides ballot disputes and whether a result can be certified, which affects trust in elections and control of Congress.

background_read: A Senate election chooses who will represent a state in the United States Senate.
Voters pick from the names printed on a ballot, so two candidates with very similar names can cause confusion.
Certification is the official step that confirms an election result.
Questions about who may appear on a state ballot are usually decided under state law, and state courts can rule on them.
